extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, inventors, and law students (those drafting or litigating patent specifications)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and legal standards for preparing a patent specification that satisfies statutory and judicial requirements (enablement, candor, claim scope, combinations vs separate inventions). Useful for drafters, litigators, and judges deciding specification sufficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claiming application of a principle vs the principle itself
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim which states will, more or less, produce the benefit, and you are not tied down to any form. ... this was not a claim to a principle, but to the construction of a chair on this principle, in whatever shape or form it may be constructed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustration: Minter's Patent (self-adjusting lever applied to a reclining chair) — claiming the application or construction implementing a principle (in whatever shape or form) can be upheld so long as it is a claim to a construction applying the principle rather than to the abstract principle alone. The practical application and disclosed means matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination claims vs separate inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: It is often necessary to decide whether the patentee claims a combination of several things, or the distinct invention of several things, or both. ... one circumstance that will always be decisive ... is, that one or more of them is not new.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If any element of a claimed set is not new, the court must consider whether the patent can be sustained for the combination only. A patent for a combination of three things cannot at the same time be a patent for a combination of any two of them. The subject-matter defined as the combination governs; sub-portions less than the whole cannot be treated as the claimed subject-matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty not to mislead the public (no concealment or deceptive additions)
rubrics_metrics.description: The patentee must not mislead the public, either by concealing anything material to the invention, or by adding anything not necessary to be introduced. The statute enacts it as one of the defences ... that the specification 'does not contain the whole truth relative to his invention or discovery, or that it contains more than is necessary to produce the described effect; which concealment or addition shall fully appear to have been made for the purpose of deceiving the public.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This defense succeeds when the patentee fraudulently concealed material information known to him or fraudulently added useless, immaterial, or unnecessary matter with intent to deceive. If something later proves not useful, patent may survive; fraudulent intent at drafting is key.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement: describe manner and process in full, clear, exact terms
rubrics_metrics.description: The statute requires the patentee to describe 'the manner and process of making, constructing, using, and compounding his invention or discovery, in such full, clear, and exact terms, avoiding unnecessary prolixity, as to enable any person skilled in the art or science ... to make, construct, compound, and use the same; and in case of any machine, he shall fully explain the principle and the several modes in which he has contemplated the application of that principle ... and shall particularly specify and point out the part, improvement, or combination which he claims as his own invention or discovery.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specification must enable a person skilled in the art to practice the invention from the specification alone; for machines the principle and modes of application must be explained; the claimed part/improvement must be particularly specified and pointed out.

rubrics_metrics.name: Person skilled in the art: practical workman of reasonably competent skill
rubrics_metrics.description: They are not those who possess the highest degree of skill or knowledge ... nor are they day-laborers; they are practical workmen, or persons of reasonably competent skill in the particular art, science, or branch of industry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The specification is judged by whether a person of ordinary, competent skill (not an expert-of-experts nor an unskilled laborer) could carry the invention into effect using the description without invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: No requirement that disclosure enable the highest-skilled person
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not necessary that the specification should contain an explanation level with the capacity of every person, which would often be impossible. The statute allows the patentee to address himself to persons of competent skill in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drafters should tailor disclosure to the ordinary competent practitioner in the field rather than to novices or only to top-tier experts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Must enable practice without invention, addition, or repeated experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: The description must be such as will enable persons of competent skill and knowledge to construct or reproduce the thing described, without invention or addition of their own, and without repeated experiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the specification requires the practitioner to set themselves a problem to solve or to invent additional features to make the invention work, the specification is insufficient. Examples: failure to state material alterations (materials, form, speed, relative dimensions) renders specification insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Slight defects that force inventive exercise vitiate patent
rubrics_metrics.description: Slight defects in a specification will sometimes prevent the object of the patent from being obtained by any competent person who may undertake to apply the description. ... As, the omitting to state the use of tallow, which the patentee employed for facilitating the manufacture of steel trusses; or, in a patent medicine, stating the ingredients without stating the proportions. If anything be omitted, which gives an advantageous operation to the thing invented, it will vitiate the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patentee is bound to give the most advantageous mode known to him and any circumstance conducive to advantageous operation. Omitting such details (e.g., a facilitating material or proportions) can invalidate the patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification must disclose how to handle injurious foreign matter or obtain proper material state
rubrics_metrics.description: If a specification directs the use of a substance which, as generally known, contains foreign matter positively injurious, and does not show any method of removing that foreign matter, or refer to any method generally known, or state how the substance in a proper state can be procured, the specification will be defective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an ingredient as ordinarily obtained is unsuitable without processing, the specification must explain or reference how to obtain it in suitable condition, or else risk invalidity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid obscure terms used for concealment
rubrics_metrics.description: If obscure terms be employed for the sake of concealment, so as to induce the belief that elaborate processes are necessary, when the simplest will succeed, the specification is bad; and if a patentee states that he prefers a certain material, having ascertained that no other will answer, he misleads the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concealment by vague/obscure language intended to mislead renders specification defective. Be clear about whether preferred materials are essential or merely preferred and why.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naming of articles: must indicate where procurable if name is misleading
rubrics_metrics.description: A specification will be defective, if an article be described by a particular name, the patentee knowing that the requisite article cannot ordinarily be procured under the name by which it is described in the specification, and it be not stated where it may be procured; because the public have not that full and precise information which they have a right to require.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a term or trade name would not commonly identify the needed material, specify how to obtain or prepare it so the public can practice the invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compositions: proportions requirement and allowance for general rules with exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: If the specification of a patent for a composition of matter is so drawn that no one can use the invention without first ascertaining by experiment the exact proportion of the different ingredients required ... the patent will be void. But the patentee may give a certain proportion as the general rule applicable to the ordinary state of the ingredients, and state other and variable proportions as exceptions to the rule, applicable to the varying states of the ingredients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For compositions, give a general rule/proportion; variable exceptions are permissible if the rule furnishes means of determining requisite proportions for differing ingredient states. Whether sufficient is a jury question based on expert evidence (see James Wood brick example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification need not recite known processes, common terms, or how to make everything used
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not necessary for the patentee to describe the mode of making everything which he uses, or detail known processes, or explain the terms appropriate to the particular art, or science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drafters need not repeat common general knowledge of the trade; they must, however, include what is necessary to enable a competent artisan to practice without invention. Distinguish between known art (need not be described) and any novel or material details (must be).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambiguity judged from perspective of skilled persons and can be factual question for jury
rubrics_metrics.description: The question whether a specification answers this requisite of the statute is a question of fact for the jury; a distinction must be taken between that sort of ambiguity which a person unacquainted with technical terms would encounter, and the ambiguity which might appear to a person skilled in the particular art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enablement and vagueness are factual inquiries. Evidence from competent practitioners is relevant; courts will assess whether specification enables a person of ordinary skill without invention or extensive experimentation.
